p: Wednesday night Jordan sat at her kitchen table in Aurora with a mug of tea going cold and the Centennial forecast open on her laptop, and for the first ten minutes it looked like a ransom note.
KAPA terminal forecast, Wednesday 9:40 PM. TAF KAPA 132320Z 1400/1424 33008KT P6SM FEW100. FM140900 VRB03KT P6SM SKC. FM141500 31010KT P6SM FEW080

She did what she always did with a call she didn't understand. She took it apart. The FAA's Aviation Weather Handbook was a free PDF, a few hundred pages longer than any protocol binder she'd ever been handed, and she read the section on terminal forecasts twice, the second time with a pen.

TAF, then the airport. Then 132320Z: the forecast was finished on the 13th at 2320 Zulu, which the handbook said was UTC, which a different website said was six hours ahead of Colorado in the summer. Then 1400/1424, good from midnight Zulu on the 14th to midnight Zulu at the end of it. They wrote midnight at the end as 24 so nobody would confuse it with the start. She liked that. It was the kind of rule a tired person had written for other tired people.

FM141500 meant from 1500 Zulu on the 14th. Nine in the morning, her time. Northwest at ten knots, more than six miles visibility, a few clouds at eight thousand feet. Her lesson was at seven. She'd be back on the ground by eight thirty, before any of it.
She texted Abby a screenshot with her decode typed underneath, line by line, the way she'd hand off a patient. The reply came at 10:06.
A text from Abby Strand. Not bad. Check it again when you wake up. A TAF is a forecast. The weather didn't read it.

Danny's green notebook sat at the other end of the table under her keys. She'd been reading it a few entries at a time, in order, and she'd only skipped ahead once. She set her alarm for 5:55 and went to bed.

At 5:55 the wind outside her bedroom window was pushing the neighbor's recycling bin up the sidewalk one lurch at a time. Jordan sat on the edge of the bed with her phone and pulled the weather before she'd put her feet on the floor.

KAPA, Thursday 5:53 AM. METAR KAPA 141153Z 31016G27KT 10SM FEW080 SCT120 12/M03 A3002 RMK AO2 PK WND 31031/1128 SLP148 T01171028. TAF KAPA 141120Z 1412/1512 31016G27KT P6SM FEW080 SCT120. FM141600 32020G32KT P6SM SCT100. FM150200 33010KT P6SM SKC

Taped inside her kneeboard was the card Abby had written for her after the carb ice lesson, in blocky marker: STUDENT LIMITS. YOURS UNTIL I SAY. WIND 15. GUSTS NO MORE THAN 10 OVER. CROSSWIND 8. YOU MAKE THE CALL. I'LL TELL YOU IF IT'S WRONG.
It was 6:00. The lesson was at 7.

She types it the way she'd call in a patient. Canceling. METAR 310 at 16 gust 27, peak 31 an hour ago. TAF has 20 gust 32 from 1600Z, that's 10 local. Over the card on every line. She hits send and sits there in her socks. Ninety seconds, about. Then the phone buzzes against her knee. That's the first smart thing you've done. No emoji, no punctuation to soften it, which from Abby is practically a hug. A second bubble: Briefing room at 8 anyway. Bring coffee. Not the gas station kind.

The briefing room window buzzed in its frame whenever a gust came over the ramp, and by 8:15 it was buzzing pretty much full time. Somebody had taped a sign over the light switch that said DO NOT TOUCH THERMOSTAT (RUSS). Abby had copied the morning METAR onto the whiteboard in red marker, all of it, and drawn a fat lopsided box around the end.
Everything after RMK. People skip it. A machine stood out on that field all night measuring this stuff for you, and people skip it. She capped the marker. AO2. And the T group. Go.

Yep. Zero's plus, one's minus, three digits each, in tenths. Up top it got rounded to 12 and M03. She writes 14.5 under the box and circles it twice, hard enough that the marker squeaks. Real spread. Remember it. One of these days some kid's going to ask you how high the clouds are and you'll get to be insufferable.
Walt came in at nine with a box of grocery store donuts, set it on the table, and didn't sit down. Russ says you canceled.

Hm. He picked up a marker, uncapped it, and wrote a METAR on the board from memory in small square capitals, the way a man writes something he's written ten thousand times. Denver, January, some year. I was on shift. Where's the ceiling?
METAR KDEN 140453Z 03011KT 3SM -SN BR SCT006 BKN012 OVC030 M01/M02 A3008

Walt caps the marker. Twelve hundred above the ground, three miles in snow. I dispatched into that more times than I can count, and I never once sent a Cessna. He takes a donut for himself, which Abby will tell her later is the closest thing to a compliment he has. On his way out he stops at the door. Danny would've gone this morning, you know. He'd have found a reason. He doesn't say whether that's praise or not.
After Walt left, Abby turned around the whiteboard, where she'd already written the morning TAF, and underlined FM141600 twice.
Last thing before the boring part. When does this start? On a watch. Not a computer.
The coffee maker gurgled. Out on the ramp a Piper Warrior was tied down so tight it rocked against its ropes like a dog that wanted to go for a walk.

Ten. She checks her phone. Which is forty one minutes from now. At 10:04 the window behind her rattles in its frame hard enough that they both look at it, and the windsock across the ramp goes from straight out to straight out and angry. Abby doesn't say anything. She doesn't have to.
Friday night Abby sent homework instead of a time.
A text from Abby Strand. Sat 7am if it's legal and smart. We're climbing to 7,500 over Bennett. Decode the DEN line for me. Why is half of it missing?
Jordan worked it out on the back of a pizza flyer. Then she stared at the gaps for a while, the way she'd stare at an empty line on a patient chart.

Yes. 3,000 is underground and 6,000 is 570 feet off the ground at DEN. No wind within 1,500 of the station, no temps within 2,500. A minute later: Bonus. Decode 30,000. Jordan subtracts 50 from 76, adds 100 to 02. 260 at 102, minus 41. Show off. See you at 7.
Twenty minutes later the club chat lit up.

A message from Russ Kim. taking biscuit to steamboat sunday morning, it's on the calendar, don't me. yes i see the airmets. they're airmets. sigmets are the scary ones. airmets are for gliders and nervous people

Jordan opened the graphical AIRMETs on the aviation weather site. Over the mountains west of Denver on Sunday morning there was a Tango box, moderate turbulence below 18,000, and a Sierra box stuck to the high terrain for mountain obscuration. She'd known Russ for about three weeks, and most of it had been skull emojis.

She types it plainly and adds: The Tango and the Sierra are both over your route Sunday. Not my call, you're the pilot. Just saying what they say. Nothing for four minutes. Then Russ: ok who taught the student to read. Walt: Nobody. She read it. Russ: fine. moving it to next weekend. bringing donuts as penance. marisol do not say anything. Marisol sends a single photo of the whiteboard: ELT BATT, boxed.

Saturday came up clear and dead calm. ATIS: minus one, dewpoint minus three. Biscuit had spent the night tied down on the ramp like always, and in the blue light before sunrise her wings had gone fuzzy. Powdered sugar. On May 16th. Colorado.
Jordan dragged a fingertip down the leading edge and it left a clean wet stripe of maroon paint. You could read the N number on the tail right through the stuff. Abby's text said ten minutes out.

They tow her to the east end of the row, where the sun clears the hangars first, and stand around in it like cows. Forty minutes. Marisol wanders over in a parka with three coffees in a cardboard tray and one of them has JORDAN written on the lid. Danny used to come out with a squeegee and a thermos of hot water. Then he'd stand there yelling at the water for freezing on the windshield. She hands it over. Sun's better. Sun doesn't need a thermos. Wheels up at 7:42, bare dry wings.

Sunday dinner was at Claire's in Parker. Burgers, on the enormous grill Danny bought the summer he decided he was a grill guy and then used maybe nine times. His orange Broncos camp chair was still folded up against the back fence with a dried leaf stuck in the hinge. It had been there since March.

Ellie was flat on her back on the trampoline in shin guards and one sock, eating a pickle. Above her the clouds were coming off the foothills in a herd, big lumpy white ones, and every last one had a bottom so flat you could've set a level on it. Same height, all of them. Like a glass shelf.
Aunt Jordan. Why are clouds flat on the bottom?
Claire looked over from the grill with the spatula in her hand. She didn't say anything. Danny had been the one for questions like this.

Getting onto a trampoline at thirty five turns out to involve a knee and some swearing under her breath. She lies down next to Ellie anyway. Okay. Driveway gets hot, right? Burns your feet. It heats up the air sitting on it, and hot air goes up. Bubble in a pot of water. But up is colder, so the bubble cools off on the way. And there's water hiding in it. Invisible. Cool it enough and, boom, you can see it. Like your breath in January. Like your breath in January. And all the bubbles around here started out about the same, so they all hit cold enough at the same height. That's your shelf. Ellie squints up at it for a while. So the shelf is made of cold. Kind of. You can figure out how high it is with a thermometer. Show me. Over at the grill Claire flips a burger she's already flipped, and her shoulders drop about an inch.

May 28th, a Thursday, and Centennial was showing off. Calm, cool, the windsock hanging like a sleeve. Out west over Evergreen, though, three long gray clouds sat stacked one on another like plates in a cupboard, not moving, edges so smooth they looked cut out with scissors. A guy fueling a Mooney had his phone up taking pictures.
KAPA, Thursday 6:53 AM. METAR KAPA 281253Z 23004KT 10SM FEW150 09/M01 A2988 RMK AO2 ACSL W-NW SLP101 T00891006
The winds aloft over the Divide were 270 at 45 at 12,000. Jordan had looked them up because now she couldn't help it. Abby was doing the walkaround. Those are pretty. Where do you want to go?

Good. Lenticulars. Forty five knots coming over the Divide, and it's sloshing on the far side like a bathtub, and under the sloshing there's rotor. Gorgeous. From Bennett. An hour of smooth air over the wheat. Jordan keeps twisting around in her seat to look at them, which costs her fifty feet on a steep turn and an eyebrow from Abby.

The first week of June turned hot. Abby moved the lessons earlier, and still, by 10 a.m. the air over the plains east of the airport was boiling up off the wheat fields. At 7,500 over Bennett, Biscuit hit a bump that lifted Jordan off the seat against her belt, and then another one, and the coffee cup in the side pocket jumped out and rolled under the rudder pedals.
It went on like that for a couple of minutes. Not dangerous. Not fun either. The airspeed needle wandering ten knots each way. Abby's pen bouncing on her kneeboard.
Nobody's reported this. We're on with Denver Approach. Give them a PIREP.

She keys the mic and it comes out almost the way Abby taught her. Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, PIREP. Over Bennett, seven thousand five hundred, Cessna One Seventy Two, moderate turbulence, last two minutes. The controller reads it back and thanks her. Thirty seconds later he passes it to a Bonanza inbound from the east. Abby writes PIREP on her kneeboard and draws a star next to it.

A cold front came down the plains on a Friday night in June, and by Saturday morning the whole city had a lid on it. Jordan woke at 5 to a world the color of dishwater. Her own street ended in gray after about four houses.

KAPA, Saturday 5:53 AM. METAR KAPA 061153Z 07009KT 2SM BR OVC004 09/08 A3021 RMK AO2 SLP232 T00890078. TAF KAPA 061120Z 0612/0712 07010KT 2SM BR OVC004. TEMPO 0612/0615 1/2SM FG OVC002. FM062000 05008KT 5SM BR BKN012. FM070100 33006KT P6SM SCT050
The lesson was at nine. Abby hadn't texted. Jordan understood by now that this was on purpose.

Canceling. East at 9, spread 1, upslope. TAF keeps the east wind till 2000Z, 2 PM. Abby: Agree. Go back to bed. Then: You're getting annoying to teach. Then: Compliment. Jordan gets back under the covers and doesn't sleep. Outside a garbage truck works its way down the block, invisible, beeping.
Saturday the 13th of June was the first true summer day. The TAF had a line Jordan read three times before she left the house.

KAPA terminal forecast, Saturday 5:20 AM. TAF KAPA 131120Z 1312/1412 VRB04KT P6SM FEW120. FM131700 09008KT P6SM SCT080. FM132000 13012G20KT P6SM SCT070 BKN120 PROB30 1320/1324 TSRA BKN060CB. FM140200 18006KT P6SM SCT120

Wheels up 10:30. By ten after twelve they were doing power off stalls over the practice area, and each time she rolled out of a clearing turn the stuff to the south had grown. One cloud over the Palmer Divide, twenty five miles off, maybe, had quit being a cloud. It was a tower now. Cauliflower on top, white as a fridge, still going up, and a gray smear hanging under one side of it with ragged strings falling out of the bottom and quitting halfway to the ground.
On an ambulance she'd have called it a scene she didn't like the look of. She knew that feeling. She'd never had it at 7,500 feet.
Abby, who'd seen it ten minutes ago, said nothing at all.

I want to go home. Your airplane. She turns north and calls the tower twelve miles out. The wind on the ATIS is still calm. They land at 12:41 on 35R and have Biscuit tied down and the gust locks in by 12:55. At 1:20, from the briefing room window, they watch a wall of brown dust come up the airport from the south and the windsock snap around to point north, and every tied down airplane on the ramp rocks on its ropes at once. Abby looks at her watch, then at the TAF on her phone. Forty minutes early, she says. Write that down somewhere.

Jordan drove to Parker with the windows down, which was a mistake for about three minutes when the outflow caught her on Parker Road and threw grit across the windshield, and then the air went cool and smelled like wet pavement, and it was the best thing she'd smelled all week.

Claire's kitchen window faced south, over the back fence and the camp chair and the neighbors' roofs, all the way to the long dark rise of the Palmer Divide. The storm was sitting right on top of it. The anvil had spread out across half the sky, flat and white, and under it the base was the color of a bruise, with rain hanging down in sheets you could see move.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Mija the news says hail in Castle Rock. Tell me you are not in that airplane.
On the ground since 12:41. At Claire's. Watching it from the kitchen. A pause, the three dots coming and going for a long time. Then: Good. Kiss Ellie. Which was, from her mother, about a paragraph.

Ellie knelt on a kitchen chair with her nose almost on the glass, counting between the flashes and the thunder. Claire stood behind her with a dish towel over her shoulder. Jordan had the green notebook on the counter. She'd brought it on purpose. She'd read ahead last night, finally, and found the page she wanted.

Danny's logbook, a page from June, six years ago. June 17. KAPA to KCOS for lunch, return via KFLY, 2.1. TAF said FM 2100 TSRA. Figured that's nine PM, I'll be home by four, easy. Reader, 2100 Zulu is THREE PM. Found this out at 3 PM over Monument with a black wall in front of me and a Bonanza on frequency asking ATC if anybody knew where the gust front was. Landed Meadow Lake. Ate vending machine peanut butter crackers in the FBO for two hours and watched it rain on my plans. Zulu is not a suggestion. Zulu is six hours from my watch. In the winter it's seven, which I will also forget.

Jordan read it out loud. Claire laughed before she got to the crackers, and then put the dish towel over her face for a second, and when she took it down she said, He called me from the vending machine. I remember. He said he was being responsible and he wanted credit for it. She looked over at Jordan. Abby texted me. I didn't know Abby had my number. It just said, she turned around early and didn't argue. That's the whole text.
Is Daddy's writing in there about clouds? Ellie said, without turning around from the window.
About a storm. He got stuck somewhere and had to wait it out.
Jordan looked down at the page. The handwriting got bigger in the part about the black wall. Some. Then he landed and ate crackers out of a machine for two hours. Which was the smart part.

Ellie chewed on that. Out over the Divide the rain was dragging itself back south, the dark flat base lifting off the hilltops like a lid coming off a pot, and way behind it there was a strip of that hard rinsed blue you only get afterward. Is the flat part the shelf?
Same shelf, Jordan said. Somebody just piled way too much on it.
Claire's hand went to the back of Ellie's chair. Then, after a second, to Jordan's shoulder, and it stayed there while the thunder grumbled off toward Kansas and the gutters ran.
A text from Abby Strand. Next week is airspace. Denver's Class B is a wedding cake upside down and you're going to learn every layer. Bring the sectional you bought and haven't opened.
